- **Funding**: CRF, Toll, NHAI bonds, Budgetary, PPP (BOT/HAM), Monetization (ToT, InvIT)
- **Status**: ~25,000 km awarded; ~18,000 km constructed (as of 2024)

**Complementarity with PM Gati Shakti**: Both are **spatial execution arms** of NMP. Sagarmala = **Maritime/EXIM logistics backbone**; Bharatmala = **Road-based domestic logistics backbone**. NMP integrates their project pipelines on GIS platform for synchronized multimodal planning (e.g., port-rail-road last-mile connectivity).

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: What are the two components of Ayushman Bharat and how do they differ in their target beneficiaries and implementation approach?
prelims.back: Ayushman Bharat has two components: (1) Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY) - provides health insurance cover of ₹5 lakh/family/year for secondary/tertiary hospitalization to ~10.74 crore poor/vulnerable families (SECC 2011 data); implemented via state health agencies, cashless at empaneled public/private hospitals. (2) Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs) - 1.5 lakh Sub-Centres/PHCs upgraded to deliver Comprehensive Primary Health Care (12 services including NCDs, mental health, ENT, ophthalmology, etc.) to entire population; operationalized by states with NHM funding, staffed by Community Health Officers (CHOs). PMJAY = insurance for hospitalization; HWCs = primary care service delivery.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: What are the key features of PMJAY regarding portability, benefit package, and IT platform?
prelims.back: PMJAY features: (1) Portability - beneficiaries can avail cashless treatment at any empaneled hospital across India (inter-state portability enabled). (2) Benefit package - 1,949 procedures across 27 specialties with pre-defined package rates; includes pre-hospitalization (3 days) and post-hospitalization (15 days) expenses; no cap on family size/age. (3) IT platform - National Health Authority (NHA) manages PMJAY via ABDM-integrated platform (Beneficiary Identification System, Transaction Management System, Hospital Empanelment Module); uses Aadhaar-based e-KYC for verification; real-time claim settlement through National Health Claims Exchange (NHCX). Funding: 60:40 Centre:State (90:10 for NE/hilly states); 100% Central for UTs without legislature.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: What is the National Digital Health Mission (Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission) and its key building blocks?
prelims.back: Launched Sept 2021, ABDM aims to create a national digital health ecosystem. Four key building blocks: (1) Health ID (ABHA - Ayushman Bharat Health Account) - unique 14-digit identifier for citizens, linked to Aadhaar/mobile; enables longitudinal health records. (2) Health Professional Registry (HPR) - verified database of doctors/nurses/paramedics. (3) Health Facility Registry (HFR) - geo-tagged registry of public/private health facilities. (4) Health Records/PHR App - citizen-controlled longitudinal health records with consent-based sharing. Additional: Unified Health Interface (UHI) for service discovery/booking; Drug Registry; ABDM Sandbox for innovation. Implemented by National Health Authority (NHA). Voluntary participation; data privacy under DPDP Act 2023 framework.

prelims.subject: Environment & Ecology
prelims.front: What are the targets and city coverage under the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP)?
prelims.back: NCAP (launched Jan 2019 by MoEFCC) targets: 20-30% reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 concentrations by 2024 (base year 2017), later extended to 40% by 2025-26. Covers 131 non-attainment cities (NACs) - cities violating NAAQS consecutively for 5 years. City-specific action plans prepared by SPCBs/ULBs; funding: ₹10,422 cr (2019-24) + XV Finance Commission grants (₹12,139 cr for 42 million-plus cities). Monitoring: PM10/PM2.5 via CAAQMS; PRANA portal tracks progress. Key sectors: vehicular, industrial, biomass burning, construction/dust, waste burning. Mid-term review (2023): 95 cities showed PM10 reduction; 18 cities met NAAQS.

prelims.subject: Environment & Ecology
prelims.front: Explain GRAP stages for Delhi-NCR and key measures under BS-VI norms for vehicular pollution control.
prelims.back:
GRAP (Graded Response Action Plan) - 4 stages based on AQI: Stage I (Poor, 201-300): stop construction/demolition >500 sqm, mechanized sweeping, ban on DG sets (except essential). Stage II (Very Poor, 301-400): enhance parking fees, augment CNG/electric buses, ban coal/firewood in hotels. Stage III (Severe, 401-450): ban BS-III petrol/BS-IV diesel 4-wheelers, close stone crushers/mining, WFH for 50% govt staff. Stage IV (Severe+, >450): ban all 4-wheelers (except EVs/CNG/BS-VI), close schools, odd-even for private vehicles.

BS-VI norms (April 2020): PM limit 4.5 mg/km (vs 25 mg/km BS-IV for diesel); NOx limit 60 mg/km (vs 250 mg/km); PN (particle number) limit 6×10¹¹/km; mandatory OBD-II, RDE testing; 10 ppm sulphur fuel. For petrol: NOx 60 mg/km (vs 80 mg/km). Reduced emissions ~80-90% for PM/NOx vs BS-IV.

prelims.subject: Environment & Ecology
prelims.front: What is the distinction between Protected Areas (PAs) and Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures (OECMs) under the 30x30 target, and how does India report these?
prelims.back: PAs: Legally designated areas (National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Conservation Reserves, Community Reserves) under Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, primarily for biodiversity conservation. OECMs: Geographically defined areas not primarily for conservation but delivering effective in-situ biodiversity conservation (e.g., sacred groves, biodiversity heritage sites, community conserved areas, defense areas, industrial estates with biodiversity plans). India has 1,014 PAs (5.43% land area) and has identified 14 OECM categories. Reporting to CBD via World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) and World Database on OECMs. India's 30x30 strategy includes expanding PA network, recognizing OECMs, and corridor connectivity.

prelims.subject: Art & Culture
prelims.front:
Match the following tribal/folk art forms with their states of origin and distinguishing features:
1. Warli
2. Madhubani
3. Gond
4. Pattachitra
States: Maharashtra, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha
Features: Geometric monochrome, Double-line border & bright natural colors, Dots/dashes & vibrant hues, Mythological narratives on cloth
prelims.back:
Correct matches:
1. Warli – Maharashtra (Palghar district) – Geometric monochrome (white on red ochre), uses basic shapes: circle (sun/moon), triangle (mountains/trees), square (sacred enclosure); ritualistic, depicts daily life, tarpa dance.
2. Madhubani/Mithila – Bihar (Madhubani district) – Double-line border, bright natural colors (indigo, turmeric, lampblack), no empty space; themes: Hindu deities, nature, social events; traditionally by women on walls/floors.
3. Gond – Madhya Pradesh (also Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Odisha) – Dots, dashes, fine lines creating texture; vibrant hues; animistic themes, flora/fauna, folklore; Pardhan Gond tradition.
4. Pattachitra – Odisha (Raghurajpur, Puri) – Mythological narratives on cloth (patta), bold outlines, floral borders, natural colors; themes: Jagannath, Krishna Leela, Ramayana; also practiced in West Bengal (Kalighat style differs).

prelims.subject: Economics
prelims.front: What is vertical devolution in fiscal federalism? How has the share of states in the divisible pool of taxes changed from the 14th to the 15th Finance Commission?
prelims.back: Vertical devolution refers to the share of net proceeds of Union taxes (divisible pool) allocated to states collectively. The 14th Finance Commission (2015-20) recommended 42% devolution (up from 32% by 13th FC). The 15th Finance Commission (2021-26) maintained 41% (1% retained for J&K and Ladakh UTs). The divisible pool excludes cesses and surcharges, which are not shared with states. This has led to a declining share of states in gross tax revenue despite higher devolution percentage, as cesses/surcharges have grown significantly.

prelims.subject: Economics
prelims.front: Distinguish between cess and surcharge. Why does the increasing reliance on cesses and surcharges undermine fiscal federalism?
prelims.back: Cess is a tax levied for a specific purpose (e.g., Health & Education Cess, GST Compensation Cess) and its proceeds are earmarked for that purpose. Surcharge is an additional charge on existing tax (e.g., income tax surcharge on high earners) and goes to the Consolidated Fund of India for general use. Both are excluded from the divisible pool. Rising share of cesses/surcharges in gross tax revenue (from ~10% in 2011-12 to ~20% in 2023-24) reduces the divisible pool, effectively reducing states' share despite Finance Commission recommendations. This violates the spirit of fiscal federalism by giving Centre unilateral revenue-raising power.

prelims.subject: Economics
prelims.front: Explain the GST compensation mechanism. What was the 'revenue gap' issue during 2020-22 and how was it resolved?
prelims.back: Under GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017, states were guaranteed 14% annual revenue growth (base year 2015-16) for 5 years (till June 2022). Shortfall was funded by GST Compensation Cess on sin/luxury goods. During COVID (2020-22), cess collections crashed, creating a revenue gap. Centre initially refused to borrow on behalf of states. Resolution: Centre borrowed ₹1.1 lakh crore (2020-21) and ₹1.59 lakh crore (2021-22) via special window, passed to states as back-to-back loans (not counted in states' fiscal deficit). Cess collection extended till March 2026 to repay this borrowing.

prelims.subject: Economics
prelims.front: What are the key differences between Government Securities (G-Secs), Treasury Bills (T-Bills), and State Development Loans (SDLs)?
prelims.back: G-Secs: Long-term debt instruments (dated securities) issued by Centre, tenure 5-40 years, pay semi-annual coupon. T-Bills: Short-term money market instruments issued by Centre, tenures 91-day, 182-day, 364-day, issued at discount, redeemed at par (zero-coupon). SDLs: Dated securities issued by State Governments to fund fiscal deficit, similar structure to G-Secs but carry slightly higher yield due to credit risk. All are sovereign guaranteed (SDLs by Centre under Article 293). G-Secs and SDLs are traded on NDS-OM; T-Bills on NDS-Call. FPIs can invest in all three under specified limits.

prelims.subject: Economics
prelims.front: What is the yield curve? Explain the recent bond market reforms in India including the Fully Accessible Route (FAR) and inclusion in global bond indices.
prelims.back: Yield curve plots yields of bonds of same credit quality but different maturities. Normal: upward sloping (long-term > short-term). Inverted: short-term > long-term (recession signal). Flat: transition phase. Key reforms: (1) Fully Accessible Route (FAR), 2020: Allows non-residents to invest in specified G-Secs without investment limits. (2) JPMorgan GBI-EM inclusion (June 2024): 23 FAR-eligible G-Secs (~$330 bn) included, expected $20-25 bn inflows. (3) Bloomberg Index inclusion (Jan 2025). (4) RBI's Retail Direct Scheme (2021): Direct G-Sec access for retail investors. (5) NDS-OM enhancements, T+1 settlement. Reforms aim to deepen bond market, diversify investor base, lower borrowing costs.

prelims.subject: Science & Technology
prelims.front: What is the Genome India Project? Discuss its objectives, implementing agency, and significance for precision medicine and bioeconomy.
prelims.back:
The Genome India Project (GIP) is a national initiative launched in January 2020 to sequence 10,000 genomes from diverse Indian populations. 

Objectives: (1) Create a comprehensive reference genome database for India's genetic diversity; (2) Enable population-specific disease risk prediction; (3) Support precision medicine and pharmacogenomics; (4) Boost bioeconomy through genomic research and innovation.

Implementing Agency: Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Ministry of Science & Technology. Coordinated by Centre for Brain Research, IISc Bengaluru, with 20+ partner institutions.

Significance: India's genetic diversity is underrepresented in global databases (which are ~80% European). GIP addresses this gap, enabling: (a) Better understanding of genetic predisposition to diseases like diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and rare genetic disorders prevalent in India; (b) Development of cost-effective diagnostics and targeted therapies; (c) Foundation for India's bioeconomy target of $300 billion by 2030; (d) Data sovereignty and ethical genomic research framework.

prelims.subject: Science & Technology
prelims.front: Explain the concept of 'Biofoundries' and their role in advancing synthetic biology and the bioeconomy. Mention India's initiatives in this domain.
prelims.back:
Biofoundries are automated, high-throughput facilities that apply engineering principles (Design-Build-Test-Learn cycles) to biological systems for rapid prototyping and scaling of synthetic biology products. They integrate robotics, AI/ML, and standardized biological parts (BioBricks) to accelerate the development of engineered organisms.

Role in Synthetic Biology & Bioeconomy: (1) Dramatically reduce time and cost of strain development for bio-manufacturing; (2) Enable rapid response to emerging needs (e.g., vaccine development, sustainable materials); (3) Support circular bioeconomy by engineering microbes for waste valorization, bioplastics, biofuels; (4) Democratize access to advanced bioengineering infrastructure.

India's Initiatives: (a) DBT has sanctioned India's first Biofoundry at the Institute of Life Sciences (ILS), Bhubaneswar (2023); (b) Proposed National Biofoundry Network under the BioE3 (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment) policy; (c) Collaboration with Global Biofoundry Alliance (GBA); (d) Focus areas: agricultural biotech, pharmaceuticals, industrial enzymes, and climate-resilient crops.

prelims.subject: Science & Technology
prelims.front: What is Synthetic Biology? Distinguish it from traditional genetic engineering. Highlight its applications and associated biosafety/biosecurity concerns.
prelims.back:
Synthetic Biology (SynBio) is an interdisciplinary field that applies engineering principles to biology to design and construct new biological parts, devices, and systems, or to redesign existing natural biological systems for useful purposes.

Distinction from Traditional Genetic Engineering:
- Traditional GE: Transfers single genes between organisms (cut-paste); limited predictability.
- SynBio: Designs/assembles standardized genetic parts (promoters, ribosome binding sites, terminators) into circuits/modules; uses computational modeling; aims for predictability, modularity, and scalability (engineering approach).

Applications: (1) Healthcare: mRNA vaccines, CAR-T cells, artemisinin production in yeast; (2) Agriculture: Nitrogen-fixing cereals, disease-resistant crops; (3) Industry: Bio-based chemicals, spider silk, bioplastics (PHA); (4) Environment: Biosensors for pollutants, plastic-degrading enzymes, carbon capture.

Concerns: (a) Biosafety: Accidental release of engineered organisms, gene drive ecological impacts; (b) Biosecurity: Dual-use research (pathogen synthesis), DNA synthesis screening; (c) Ethical: Human genome editing, chimeras; (d) Equity: Benefit-sharing, access to technology. India regulates via Recombinant DNA Safety Guidelines (1990, updated), GEAC, and IBSCs.

prelims.subject: Environment & Ecology
prelims.front: What are the key goals and targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF)? Explain the '30x30' target and its implications for India.
prelims.back:
The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) was adopted at CBD COP15 (Dec 2022) with 4 long-term goals for 2050 and 23 action-oriented targets for 2030.

4 Goals (2050): (A) Ecosystem integrity/connectivity; (B) Sustainable use of biodiversity; (C) Fair benefit-sharing (Nagoya Protocol); (D) Means of implementation (finance, capacity, technology).

Key 2030 Targets:
- Target 1: Spatial planning to reduce biodiversity loss
- Target 2: Restore 30% degraded ecosystems
- Target 3: **30x30** – Conserve 30% land, waters, seas through protected areas (PAs) and OECMs
- Target 4: Halt species extinction, recover threatened species
- Target 7: Reduce pollution (pesticides, plastics, nutrients)
- Target 10: Sustainable agriculture/aquaculture/forestry
- Target 19: Mobilize $200B/year; $30B/year international finance to developing countries

30x30 Target (Target 3): Effectively conserve and manage ≥30% of terrestrial, inland water, coastal and marine areas by 2030 through ecologically representative, well-connected systems of PAs and Other Effective area-based Conservation Measures (OECMs), recognizing indigenous territories.

Implications for India: India currently has ~22% terrestrial (PAs ~5.28%, plus community reserves, conservation reserves) and ~0.3% marine area under protection. Achieving 30x30 requires: (a) Expanding PA network; (b) Recognizing OECMs (sacred groves, community conserved areas, biodiversity heritage sites); (c) Integrating biodiversity in sectoral policies; (d) Enhanced finance – India advocated for $100B/year global biodiversity fund at COP15.

prelims.subject: Environment & Ecology
prelims.front: Discuss India's National Biodiversity Action Plan (NBAP) and its alignment with the Kunming-Montreal GBF. What are the key focus areas and implementation mechanisms?
prelims.back:
India's National Biodiversity Action Plan (NBAP) was first prepared in 2008 (aligned with CBD 2010 targets) and updated in 2014 (Addendum) for 2011-2020 Aichi Targets. A post-2020 NBAP aligned with Kunming-Montreal GBF is under finalization.

Current NBAP (2014 Addendum) – 12 National Biodiversity Targets (NBTs) mapped to Aichi Targets:
1. Biodiversity awareness
2. Biodiversity values integrated in planning
3. Incentives reformed
4. Sustainable production/consumption
5. Habitat loss halved
6. Sustainable fisheries
7. Sustainable agriculture
8. Pollution reduced
9. Invasive species managed
10. Climate change impacts minimized
11. Protected areas expanded (17% terrestrial, 10% marine)
12. Species extinction prevented

Alignment with GBF: The updated NBAP (expected 2024-25) will map 12 NBTs to 23 GBF targets, adding: 30x30 (Target 3), restoration (Target 2), pollution halving (Target 7), $200B finance (Target 19), gender equality (Target 23).

Implementation Mechanisms:
- National Level: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) – nodal agency
- State Level: State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) – State Biodiversity Action Plans (SBAPs)
- Local Level: Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) – People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs)
- Legal Framework: Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023) – access & benefit sharing (ABS), threatened species protection
- Finance: National/State Biodiversity Funds; CAMPA; Green Credit Programme; International finance (GEF, GCF).

prelims.subject: Science & Technology
prelims.front: What are the distinct roles of IN-SPACe, NSIL, and ISRO in India's reformed space sector? How do Skyroot Aerospace and Agnikul Cosmos fit into this ecosystem?
prelims.back: IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center) is the single-window, independent nodal agency for authorizing and regulating private space activities. NSIL (NewSpace India Limited) is the commercial arm of ISRO, responsible for marketing spin-off technologies, launch services (e.g., PSLV, SSLV), and satellite transponders. ISRO focuses on R&D, strategic missions, and capacity building. Skyroot Aerospace (Vikram-S, Vikram-1) and Agnikul Cosmos (Agnibaan) are private launch vehicle startups authorized by IN-SPACe, utilizing ISRO facilities (test ranges, tracking) and aiming for commercial small-satellite launches.

prelims.subject: Science & Technology
prelims.front: Explain Kessler Syndrome. What are the current international guidelines and Indian initiatives for space debris mitigation?
prelims.back: Kessler Syndrome is a theoretical cascade where collisions between space objects generate debris faster than atmospheric drag removes it, rendering certain orbits unusable. Key guidelines: UN COPUOS Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines (2007), IADC guidelines — limit debris release, prevent on-orbit breakups, post-mission disposal (25-year rule for LEO). India: ISRO's NETRA (Network for Space Object Tracking and Analysis) for SSA; ISRO follows IADC norms (passivation, orbit lowering); signed Artemis Accords (debris mitigation commitment); IN-SPACe mandates debris mitigation plans for private missions.

prelims.subject: Environment & Ecology
prelims.front: What are the targets under the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) and how does the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) for Delhi-NCR operate across its four stages?
prelims.back: NCAP (launched 2019): Target — 40% reduction in PM10/PM2.5 by 2025-26 (base 2017), covering 131 non-attainment cities. City-specific action plans, monitoring, source apportionment. GRAP (CAQM, 2021): Stage I (AQI Poor 201-300) — ban on coal/firewood, strict dust control. Stage II (Very Poor 301-400) — enhance parking fees, augment public transport, DG set restrictions. Stage III (Severe 401-450) — ban on construction, BS-III petrol/BS-IV diesel 4-wheelers, brick kilns. Stage IV (Severe+ >450) — ban on non-essential trucks, 4-wheelers (odd-even), work-from-home advisory.

prelims.subject: Environment & Ecology
prelims.front: What are the key technological and policy solutions promoted to address stubble burning in Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh?
prelims.back: In-situ: Happy Seeder, Super SMS, Paddy Straw Chopper, Mulcher, Rotavator — incorporate residue into soil (subsidized 50-80% under CRM scheme). Ex-situ: Biomass power plants, 2G ethanol (e.g., Panipat), compressed biogas (SATAT), pelletization for co-firing in thermal plants (NTPC mandate 5-10% biomass). Policy: Crop diversification (Maize, Cotton, Pulses via MSP assurance), direct seeding of rice (DSR) to advance harvest, ex-gratia cash incentive (₹2,500/acre in Punjab/Haryana), PUSA Decomposer (microbial spray). Monitoring via satellite (ICAR/NASA).

prelims.subject: Environment & Ecology
prelims.front: Compare BS-IV and BS-VI emission norms for diesel and petrol vehicles. What technological changes were mandated for the leapfrog from BS-IV to BS-VI in 2020?
prelims.back: BS-VI (2020) vs BS-IV (2017): PM limit — diesel: 4.5 mg/km (BS-VI) vs 25 mg/km (BS-IV), 80% cut; NOx — diesel: 80 mg/km vs 250 mg/km, 68% cut; petrol: 60 mg/km vs 80 mg/km. PN (particle number) limit introduced: 6×10¹¹/km (diesel & direct-injection petrol). Technologies: Diesel — DPF (Diesel Particulate Filter), LNT/SCR (Selective Catalytic Reduction with AdBlue/urea), advanced EGR. Petrol — GPF (Gasoline Particulate Filter) for GDI engines, improved three-way catalysts. On-board diagnostics (OBD-II) mandatory. Fuel: 10 ppm sulphur (vs 50 ppm). Leapfrogged BS-V entirely.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: What are the key features and target beneficiaries of the Stand Up India Scheme, and how does it differ from the MUDRA Scheme?
prelims.back: Stand Up India (launched 2016) provides bank loans between ₹10 lakh and ₹1 crore to at least one SC/ST borrower and one woman borrower per bank branch for setting up greenfield enterprises in manufacturing, services, or trading. The borrower must hold ≥51% stake. MUDRA (Micro Units Development & Refinance Agency, 2015) provides refinance support to banks/MFIs for loans up to ₹10 lakh (Shishu: ≤₹50k, Kishor: ₹50k-₹5L, Tarun: ₹5L-₹10L) to non-corporate, non-farm small/micro enterprises. Key difference: Stand Up India targets SC/ST & women for greenfield projects (₹10L-₹1Cr), while MUDRA is for all micro enterprises (up to ₹10L) including existing ones.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: Explain the Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS) under Startup India: its corpus, management, investment strategy, and key eligibility criteria for startups to benefit.
prelims.back: FFS (established 2016) has a corpus of ₹10,000 crore (contributed over 14th & 15th Finance Commission cycles). Managed by SIDBI, it invests in SEBI-registered Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) which in turn invest in startups. FFS does not invest directly. Eligibility: DPIIT-recognized startup, incorporated as private limited/LLP/partnership, turnover <₹100 crore, up to 10 years from incorporation, working towards innovation/improvement of products/services/processes. As of 2023, FFS has committed ~₹7,500 crore to 100+ AIFs, catalyzing ~₹50,000 crore+ investment.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: What is the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) and how has it transformed public procurement? Mention its key features, mandatory use provisions, and recent expansions.
prelims.back: GeM (launched 2016) is a 100% government-owned online platform for transparent, efficient public procurement of goods/services. Key features: e-bidding, reverse auction, demand aggregation, vendor rating, integrated payment system. Mandatory for all Central Ministries/Departments (Rule 149 of GFR 2017). States/UTs onboarded via MoUs. Expansions: GeM 3.0 (2020) added services, lease/hire, composite bids; GeM 4.0 (2022) introduced AI/ML analytics, unified vendor registration. As of 2023, >₹3 lakh crore GMV, 63 lakh+ sellers, 58,000+ buyer organizations. Savings estimated at 15-20% over traditional procurement.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: Compare Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) and AMRUT 2.0: their objectives, coverage, funding pattern, and key performance indicators.
prelims.back: JJM (2019): Objective - Functional Household Tap Connection (FHTC) to every rural household by 2024. Coverage: Rural only. Funding: Centre:State = 90:10 (Himalayan/NE), 50:50 (other states), 100% UT. KPIs: FHTC coverage, water quality testing, source sustainability. AMRUT 2.0 (2021): Objective - Universal water supply (tap connections) in all 4,700+ statutory towns; sewerage/septage management; water body rejuvenation. Coverage: Urban only. Funding: Centre:State = 50:50 (million+ cities), 1/3:2/3 (other cities), 90:10 (NE/Himalayan), 100% UT. KPIs: Tap connections, sewerage coverage, non-revenue water reduction (<20%), water body rejuvenation. Both emphasize community participation and water quality surveillance.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: What are the key components and funding mechanisms of Swachh Bharat Mission 2.0 (Urban) and how does it differ from SBM 1.0?
prelims.back: SBM-U 2.0 (2021-26, ₹1.41 lakh crore) focuses on: (1) 100% scientific waste management (source segregation, collection, processing, disposal), (2) Wastewater treatment (faecal sludge & sewage), (3) Legacy dumpsite remediation, (4) Construction & Demolition waste management, (5) Plastic waste management. Funding: Centre:State = 90:10 (NE/Himalayan), 60:40 (other states), 100% UT. Private sector participation encouraged via PPP. Differences from SBM 1.0 (2014-19): Shift from ODF focus to ODF+/ODF++/Water+; mandatory source segregation; focus on circular economy (waste to wealth); remediation of all legacy dumpsites; digital tracking (SBM-U dashboard); ULB-wise action plans with measurable outcomes.

prelims.subject: Science & Technology
prelims.front: Compare India's approach to AI governance with the EU AI Act. What are the key philosophical and regulatory differences?
prelims.back: India follows a **pro-innovation, risk-based, sectoral approach** (MeitY advisories, DPDP Act, sectoral regulators like RBI/SEBI/TRAI), avoiding a single horizontal law. The **EU AI Act (2024)** is a **comprehensive horizontal legislation** classifying AI by risk (unacceptable, high, limited, minimal) with strict compliance, conformity assessments, and heavy fines (up to 7% global turnover). Key differences: (1) India = voluntary guidelines + existing laws; EU = binding regulation. (2) India prioritizes innovation & digital public infrastructure (DPI) integration; EU prioritizes fundamental rights & consumer protection. (3) India's MeitY advisory (Mar 2024) requires govt permission for 'unreliable' AI models — later diluted to self-labeling; EU mandates third-party audits for high-risk AI. (4) India chairs Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) 2024, pushing Global South perspective; EU sets global regulatory benchmark (Brussels Effect).

prelims.subject: Science & Technology
prelims.front: How does India regulate deepfakes and synthetic media? Trace the evolution from IT Rules 2021 to recent MeitY advisories.
prelims.back: India lacks a standalone deepfake law. Regulation evolved through: (1) **IT Rules 2021 (Intermediary Guidelines)**: Rule 3(1)(b) — intermediaries must remove morphed/impersonation content within 24 hrs of complaint; Rule 4(2) — significant social media intermediaries (SSMIs) must enable traceability of originator. (2) **Nov 2023 MeitY Advisory**: Directed platforms to identify & remove deepfakes within 36 hrs, appoint grievance officers, and label AI-generated content. (3) **Mar 2024 MeitY Advisory**: Required explicit govt permission for deploying 'unreliable/under-testing' AI models — withdrawn after industry backlash; replaced by **self-regulatory labeling** (watermarking, metadata, disclaimers). (4) **DPDP Act 2023**: Addresses non-consensual use of personal data for deepfakes. (5) **Bharat 6G Vision & IndiaAI Mission**: Fund R&D for deepfake detection tools. Gaps: No criminal liability for creators (only Sec 66D IT Act — cheating by personation), no mandatory watermarking standards, enforcement relies on intermediary compliance.

prelims.subject: Science & Technology
prelims.front: What are the seven principles of 'Ethical AI' outlined in NITI Aayog's 'Responsible AI for All' (2021) and how do they operationalize in India's governance framework?
prelims.back: NITI Aayog's **7 Principles**: (1) **Safety & Reliability** — robust testing, fail-safes; (2) **Equality** — non-discrimination, bias mitigation; (3) **Inclusivity & Non-discrimination** — access for marginalized, multilingual; (4) **Privacy & Security** — data minimization, consent (aligned with DPDP Act); (5) **Transparency** — explainability, algorithmic audit trails; (6) **Accountability** — human-in-the-loop, liability frameworks; (7) **Protection of Human Values** — autonomy, dignity, constitutional morality. **Operationalization**: MeitY's **IndiaAI Mission** (₹10,372 Cr) embeds these via — **AI Safety Institute** (standard-setting, red-teaming), **Responsible AI Toolkit** (bias detection, fairness metrics), **Sectoral Sandboxes** (health, agri, fintech) with ethical guardrails, **Global IndiaAI Summit 2024** consensus on 'AI for All'. Challenges: Principles are advisory; no statutory enforcement; sectoral regulators (RBI, ICMR, SEBI) interpret differently.

prelims.subject: International Relations
prelims.front: Analyze the significance of the Voice of Global South Summit (VOGSS) hosted by India. How does it reflect India's 'bridge' strategy between Global North and South?
prelims.back: **VOGSS** (Jan 2023 & Nov 2023, virtual) — India's flagship initiative to **amplify Global South priorities** (125+ countries) without Northern dominance. **Significance**: (1) **Agenda-setting**: Focus on development, climate finance, debt, digital divide, food/energy security — issues sidelined in G7/G20. (2) **Institutional innovation**: No permanent secretariat; low-cost, inclusive, leader-driven. (3) **G20 Presidency feedstock**: VOGSS outcomes (e.g., 'Development Compact') directly shaped New Delhi Leaders' Declaration (African Union membership, MDB reform, digital public infrastructure). **Bridge Strategy**: India leverages **dual membership** (G20, BRICS, SCO, Quad) to translate Southern demands into Northern forums. Examples: (a) Pushed **MDB capital adequacy reform** (G20 Independent Expert Group) echoing VOGSS debt distress calls. (b) Championed **DPI transfer** (UPI, Aadhaar, CoWIN) as Southern public good. (c) Mediated **G20 consensus on Ukraine** (para on territorial integrity) by balancing Western pressure & Southern neutrality. Limitation: No binding commitments; implementation depends on Northern political will.

prelims.subject: International Relations
prelims.front: What are the three pillars of 'Development Finance Reform' advocated by India for the Global South? Explain with reference to MDB evolution and the Bridgetown Initiative.
prelims.back: India's **three pillars** (articulated in G20, VOGSS, UNGA): (1) **Scale & Terms**: **Expand MDB lending capacity** via capital adequacy framework reform (G20 Expert Group: $200B additional headroom over 10 yrs), **concessional finance** for LICs/LMICs, longer maturities, lower interest. (2) **Responsiveness**: **Faster disbursement**, crisis triggers (pandemic, climate), **debt pause clauses** (hurricane/clause) — aligned with **Bridgetown Initiative 2.0** (Barbados PM Mottley). (3) **Representation & Governance**: **Voice reform** — quota/shareholding realignment for Global South; **country platforms** for programmatic (not project) lending. **MDB Evolution**: World Bank's 'Evolution Roadmap' (2023) adopts: hybrid capital, callable capital activation, portfolio guarantees, single-project → programmatic. **India's role**: Co-chairs G20 MDB Expert Group; pushes **IDA21 replenishment** ($100B+); advocates **regional MDBs** (AIIB, NDB) as alternatives; demands **climate finance** not counted as ODA. Challenge: Northern shareholders (US, EU, Japan) resist quota loss; capital increases need legislative approvals.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: What are the key structural changes in school education under NEP 2020, and how does the 5+3+3+4 pedagogical structure differ from the previous 10+2 system?
prelims.back: NEP 2020 replaces 10+2 with 5+3+3+4 structure: Foundational (5 years: 3 years Anganwadi/pre-school + Grades 1-2), Preparatory (3 years: Grades 3-5), Middle (3 years: Grades 6-8), Secondary (4 years: Grades 9-12). Key changes: Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) formalized; multidisciplinary, holistic education; vocational integration from Grade 6; board exams reformed (twice a year, modular); 3-language formula with flexibility; National Curriculum Framework for four stages; PARAKH for assessment standards.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: Explain the higher education reforms under NEP 2020, focusing on the four-tier institutional architecture, HECI, and the Academic Bank of Credits.
prelims.back: NEP 2020 higher education reforms: (1) Four-tier architecture: Research Universities, Teaching Universities, Autonomous Degree Colleges, Community Colleges. (2) HECI (Higher Education Commission of India) with four verticals: NHERC (regulation), NAC (accreditation), HEGC (funding), GEC (standards). (3) Academic Bank of Credits (ABC) - digital repository for credit transfer, multiple entry/exit, degrees after 1/2/3/4 years. (4) Multidisciplinary Education and Research Universities (MERUs) at par with IITs/IIMs. (5) Phasing out affiliating system; graded autonomy. (6) National Research Foundation (NRF) for research funding.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: What are the objectives and key features of the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes? How many sectors are covered and what is the total outlay?
prelims.back: PLI schemes (launched 2020-21) aim to: boost domestic manufacturing, attract investment, enhance exports, create jobs, reduce import dependence. Key features: incentive on incremental sales (4-6% typically) over base year for 5 years; greenfield/brownfield investments eligible; minimum investment & sales thresholds. Covers 14 sectors with total outlay ~₹1.97 lakh crore: (1) Mobile manufacturing, (2) Critical key starting materials/Drug Intermediates/APIs, (3) Medical devices, (4) Automobiles & auto components, (5) Pharmaceuticals, (6) Specialty steel, (7) Telecom & networking, (8) Electronic/technology products, (9) White goods (ACs/LEDs), (10) Food processing, (11) Textiles (MMF/technical textiles), (12) Drones & components, (13) Advanced chemistry cell (ACC) batteries, (14) Solar PV modules.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: Identify the PLI scheme beneficiaries and outcomes for the electronics/telecom and pharmaceutical sectors. What are the investment and production targets?
prelims.back: Electronics/Telecom: Beneficiaries - global majors (Apple vendors Foxconn, Wistron, Pegatron; Samsung, Dixon, Lava, Bhagwati). Outcomes: Mobile production ₹3.5 lakh crore (FY23), exports ₹90,000+ crore; 800,000+ jobs. Telecom: 42 companies approved, ₹3,345 crore investment. Pharmaceuticals: 55 selected applicants (38 APIs, 17 formulations); committed investment ₹15,000+ crore; incremental sales target ₹2.94 lakh crore; 200,000+ jobs. Key outcome: reduced import dependence on China for APIs (from ~70% to ~50%).

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: How is NEP 2020 being implemented? Describe the roles of NEP Implementation Committees, SARTHAQ, and the National Curriculum Framework (NCF) 2023.
prelims.back: Implementation architecture: (1) National Steering Committee (Chair: Education Minister) for oversight. (2) National Mission for Mentoring. (3) SARTHAQ (Students' and Teachers' Holistic Advancement through Quality Education) - 297 tasks with timelines, responsible agencies, outputs. (4) NCF 2023 for Foundational Stage (launched Oct 2022) and School Education (Aug 2023) - guides textbook development, pedagogy, assessment. (5) Vidya Pravesh (3-month play-based school prep for Grade 1). (6) NIPUN Bharat for foundational literacy/numeracy by Grade 3 (2026-27). (7) PM SHRI schools (14,500 model schools). (8) PARAKH for assessment reform. (9) State/UT level committees for localization.

prelims.subject: Environment & Ecology
prelims.front: What are the key mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, and how do they differ from the Kyoto Protocol's Clean Development Mechanism (CDM)?
prelims.back: Article 6 establishes three voluntary cooperation mechanisms: (1) Article 6.2 — Cooperative Approaches: Allows bilateral/regional transfer of mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) with corresponding adjustments to avoid double counting; no central UN oversight. (2) Article 6.4 — Mechanism: Successor to CDM, supervised by a UN body; generates A6.4ERs (emission reductions) with mandatory corresponding adjustments and share of proceeds for adaptation. (3) Article 6.8 — Non-Market Approaches: Framework for cooperation without carbon markets (e.g., technology transfer, capacity building). Key differences from CDM: mandatory corresponding adjustments (no double counting), overall mitigation in global emissions (OMGE) requirement, stronger sustainability safeguards, and transition of CDM projects subject to host country approval.

prelims.subject: Environment & Ecology
prelims.front: Explain the Loss and Damage Fund established at COP27 and operationalized at COP28. What are its governance structure, funding sources, and eligibility criteria?
prelims.back: The Loss and Damage Fund (LDF) was established at COP27 (Sharm El-Sheikh) and operationalized at COP28 (Dubai). Governance: Hosted by World Bank as interim trustee (4 years); governed by a 26-member Board (12 developed, 14 developing countries); independent secretariat. Funding: Voluntary contributions from developed countries and others 'in a position to do so'; innovative sources encouraged (levies, taxes). No mandatory assessed contributions. Eligibility: All developing countries 'particularly vulnerable' to climate change; access via National Designated Authorities; focus on economic and non-economic losses (slow-onset events, extreme weather). Key principle: Not liability/compensation (per Decision 2/CP.27). Initial pledges ~$700M (UAE, Germany, EU, UK, US, Japan).

prelims.subject: Environment & Ecology
prelims.front: What is the Global Stocktake (GST) under the Paris Agreement? Describe its process, components, and the key outcomes of the first GST at COP28.
prelims.back: Global Stocktake (Article 14) is a 5-yearly collective assessment of progress toward Paris goals (mitigation, adaptation, finance). Process: Three phases — (1) Information collection (IPCC reports, Party submissions), (2) Technical assessment (structured expert dialogues), (3) Consideration of outputs (political phase at COP). First GST concluded at COP28 (Dubai) with 'UAE Consensus'. Key outcomes: (a) Mitigation: Call to 'transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems' (first explicit mention), triple renewables & double energy efficiency by 2030, accelerate zero/low-emission tech. (b) Adaptation: Framework for Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) with targets on water, health, ecosystems. (c) Finance: Urge developed countries to double adaptation finance by 2025; new collective quantified goal (NCQG) post-2025. (d) Loss & Damage: Operationalize fund. Next GST: 2028.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: Compare Startup India, Stand Up India, and MUDRA Yojana in terms of target beneficiaries, financial support, and key objectives.
prelims.back: Startup India (2016): Targets DPIIT-recognized startups (innovation-driven, scalable). Support: Tax holiday (3/7 years), 80% patent fee rebate, self-certification, Fund of Funds (₹10,000 Cr via SIDBI), credit guarantee. Objective: Foster innovation ecosystem. Stand Up India (2016): Targets SC/ST and women entrepreneurs (1 per bank branch). Support: Bank loans ₹10 lakh–₹1 crore for greenfield enterprises (manufacturing/services/trading); composite loan (term + working capital); margin money 25% (convergence with state schemes). Objective: Promote entrepreneurship among marginalized. MUDRA (2015): Targets non-corporate, non-farm micro/small enterprises. Support: Collateral-free loans up to ₹20 lakh (enhanced from ₹10 lakh in 2024) under three categories — Shishu (≤₹50K), Kishor (₹50K–₹5L), Tarun (₹5L–₹20L); delivered via banks/NBFCs/MFIs. Objective: Fund the unfunded, formalize credit access.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: What is the Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS) and the Government e-Marketplace (GeM)? Explain their structure, operation, and impact.
prelims.back: Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS): Established 2016 under Startup India; corpus ₹10,000 Cr (contributed over 14th/15th Finance Commission cycles). Operated by SIDBI. Structure: FFS → invests in SEBI-registered Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) → AIFs invest in DPIIT-recognized startups. Government does not invest directly. Focus: Early-stage, risk capital. Impact: As of 2024, ~₹8,000+ Cr committed to 100+ AIFs, supporting 1,000+ startups. Government e-Marketplace (GeM): Launched 2016; 100% government-owned SPV under Ministry of Commerce. Online platform for public procurement (goods/services) by Central/State govts, PSUs, autonomous bodies. Features: Transparent, cashless, contactless; reverse auction, e-bidding; mandatory for common-use goods/services (GFR 2017). Impact: >₹4 lakh crore GMV; 1.5 lakh+ sellers (60%+ MSMEs); estimated savings 15–20%; integrated with PPP (Public Procurement Portal) for vendor assessment.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: What are the key features, eligibility criteria, and funding pattern of PM-KISAN (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi) scheme?
prelims.back: PM-KISAN: Central Sector Scheme (100% GoI funded) launched Feb 2019. Provides ₹6,000/year in three equal installments of ₹2,000 directly to bank accounts of eligible farmer families. Eligibility: All landholding farmer families (husband, wife, minor children) with cultivable land. Exclusions: Institutional landholders, former/present constitutional post holders, ministers, MPs/MLAs, serving/retired government employees (except Group D/Multi-tasking), professionals (doctors, engineers, lawyers, CAs), income tax payees. Implemented via PM-KISAN portal with Aadhaar-seeded database. As of 2024, over 11 crore beneficiaries covered.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: Explain the structure, premium rates, and claim settlement mechanism of Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY).
prelims.back: PMFBY (launched 2016): Crop insurance scheme replacing NAIS/MNAIS. Premium rates: Kharif crops 2%, Rabi crops 1.5%, Annual commercial/horticultural crops 5%. Farmer share capped; balance shared 50:50 by Centre and State (90:10 for NE/hilly states). Covers yield losses (prevented sowing, mid-season adversity, post-harvest losses up to 14 days). Implemented by empanelled insurance companies via bidding. Claim settlement: Based on Crop Cutting Experiments (CCEs) at Gram Panchayat level. Technology-driven: Smartphones for CCEs, remote sensing, drones for area estimation. Revamped 2020: Voluntary for farmers, States can choose risk coverage, central subsidy capped at 30% for unirrigated/25% for irrigated areas.

prelims.subject: Government Schemes
prelims.front: What are e-NAM and Soil Health Card Scheme? How do they address agricultural marketing and soil fertility issues?
prelims.back: e-NAM (National Agriculture Market, launched 2016): Pan-India electronic trading platform networking existing APMC mandis. Objectives: Unified national market, price discovery via transparent auction, reduce intermediaries, ensure better prices. Features: Single license for traders, single point market fee, electronic weighing/assaying, online payment. As of 2024: 1,389 mandis across 23 States/4 UTs integrated. Soil Health Card Scheme (launched 2015): Provides farmers crop-wise nutrient/fertilizer recommendations based on soil testing. Tests 12 parameters: pH, EC, OC, N, P, K, S, Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B. Cards issued every 2 years. Implemented via GPS-enabled soil sampling. Helps balanced fertilizer use, reduces input cost, improves soil health. Both schemes promote digital agriculture and sustainable farming.

prelims.subject: Art & Culture
prelims.front: Compare Warli (Maharashtra) and Madhubani/Mithila (Bihar) paintings - themes, techniques, colors, and social context.
prelims.back: Warli (Maharashtra, Warli tribe): Monochromatic - white pigment (rice paste + gum) on red ochre/mud walls. Geometric shapes: circle (sun/moon), triangle (mountains/trees), square (sacred enclosure). Themes: Daily life - farming, hunting, fishing, festivals, dances (tarpa), marriage rituals. No mythological/religious figures. Ritualistic: Painted by married women (suvasinis) during weddings/harvest. Madhubani/Mithila (Bihar, Mithila region): Traditionally on walls/floors (aripana), now paper/cloth. Bright natural colors: red (kusum flower), yellow (turmeric), blue (indigo), green (leaves), black (soot), white (rice powder). Double line border, no empty space (filled with flora/fauna). Themes: Hindu deities (Krishna, Rama, Durga), celestial bodies, royal court, social events. Styles: Bharni (filled), Kachni (line), Tantrik, Godna, Kohbar. Originally by Brahmin/Kayastha women; now widespread. Both GI-tagged.

prelims.subject: Art & Culture
prelims.front: Describe Gond painting (Madhya Pradesh) and Pattachitra (Odisha/West Bengal) - distinctive features, materials, themes, and cultural significance.
prelims.back: Gond (Madhya Pradesh, Gond tribe): 'Gond' from 'Kond' (green mountains). Traditionally on walls/floors during festivals; now canvas/paper. Signature: Fine dots, dashes, lines creating texture/movement. Bright colors (earlier natural: charcoal, plant sap, cow dung; now acrylic). Themes: Nature worship - trees, animals, birds; folk tales; deities (Phulvari Devi, Bada Dev); daily life. 'Signature patterns' unique to each artist (e.g., Jangarh Singh Shyam pioneered modern Gond). Pattachitra (Odisha: Raghurajpur; West Bengal: Medinipur): 'Patta' (cloth) + 'Chitra' (picture). Canvas: Old cotton cloth coated with tamarind seed paste + chalk powder. Natural colors: Hingula (red), Haritala (yellow), Ramaraja (blue), Kala (black from lamp soot), Sankha (white from conch). Themes: Jagannath cult (Badhia, Krishnalila, Dasavatar), Ramayana, Mahabharata, folk tales. Distinctive: Floral borders, no perspective, profile faces with elongated eyes. Hereditary chitrakar families. Both GI-tagged; Gond also has state recognition.

mains.subject: Essay Tips
mains.front: Key Essay Writing Tips for UPSC Mains
mains.back: 1) Choose topic you know well 2) Structure: Intro (hook+thesis), Body (social/economic/political/philosophical dimensions), Conclusion (way forward) 3) Use quotes, examples, data 4) Balance views 5) Focus paragraphs 6) ~1200-1500 words 7) Legible handwriting

mains.subject: Answer Writing
mains.back: Intro (30 words): Define/contextualize. Body (180 words): Multiple dimensions, examples, data, committee recommendations. Use headings/bullets. Conclusion (40 words): Way forward. Key: Answer what is ASKED (discuss/analyze/critically examine are different demands).

mains.subject: GS-II Concepts
mains.back: Cooperative: Centre+states work together (GST Council, NITI Aayog, Inter-State Council). Competitive: States compete for investment/governance (EoDB rankings, SDG Index). India practices both. Issues: GST compensation, freebies, Governor controversies.

mains.subject: GS-III Concepts
mains.back: Growth benefiting all, especially marginalized. Indicators: poverty reduction, lower inequality (Gini), improved social indicators. Approach: MGNREGA, JAM Trinity, DBT, skill development. Challenges: 90% informal employment, regional disparities, gender gap.

interview.subject: Interview Prep
interview.back: Every word is potential question material. Prepare: 1) Hometown/state issues 2) Education relevance to admin 3) Hobbies (in-depth) 4) Work experience achievements 5) Optional subject relevance 6) Service/cadre preference reasons. Have 3-4 talking points each.

interview.subject: Interview Prep
interview.back: Acceptable to say you don't know - honesty valued. Say: 'I'm not sure about specifics, but based on my understanding...' NEVER bluff. Can request: 'May I think about this?' Shows composure. Follow up with what you DO know on the topic.

interview.subject: Interview Prep
interview.back: 1) Firm handshake 2) Eye contact with ALL panelists 3) Upright but relaxed 4) Natural gestures sparingly 5) Genuine smile 6) Don't fidget/cross arms 7) Nod to show listening 8) Breathe before answering 9) Thank panel at end
